oil.summary: Crude prices traded in a narrow range on the day — WTI edged fractionally lower to $75.99/bbl while Brent firmed 0.84% to $79.62 — but the month-long collapse of roughly 29-30% dominates the tape. The dominant driver remains the US-Iran ceasefire framework, due to be signed in Geneva on June 19, which has unlocked Strait of Hormuz traffic: tankers previously diverted to Africa are reversing course and Iran's first crude exports in two months have already cleared the US blockade. Falling Murban and Dubai benchmarks are opening arbitrage windows to Western buyers. Bearish supply-side pressure is partially offset by a larger-than-expected 8.3 million barrel draw in US crude inventories per EIA, escalating G7 and EU sanctions on Russian oil revenues, and TotalEnergies flagging that a key Saudi refinery will not fully recover until early 2027. RBOB gasoline fell the sharpest on the day, down 2.21%.
drivers: US-Iran deal and Hormuz reopening flooding market with returning supply, crashing Middle East benchmark prices and enabling trans-ocean arbitrage
US crude inventories drew 8.3 million barrels for the week ending June 12, providing a modest demand-side cushion against the broader selloff
G7 and EU escalation of sanctions on Russian oil revenues adds geopolitical uncertainty to the supply picture, though near-term price impact is overshadowed by the Iran normalization

gas.summary: Natural gas markets saw divergent moves: Henry Hub slipped 2.32% on the day to $3.164/MMBtu, though it remains up 4.63% on the month, while European TTF fell 0.74% to €41.46/MWh and is down sharply — over 17% — on both the week and month. Two simultaneous supply-side relief events weighed on TTF: the Ichthys LNG strike in Australia has ended after unions and operator Inpex reached an agreement, and Qatar is repositioning LNG tankers toward the Middle East ahead of an imminent Hormuz reopening, signalling a resumption of Qatari LNG exports that were disrupted during the Iran crisis. ExxonMobil's preliminary agreement to supply South Africa's first LNG import terminal points to incremental long-term demand, while G7 sanctions on Russian gas exports remain a structural upside tail risk for European prices.
drivers: Ichthys LNG strike resolution in Australia removes a weeks-long supply disruption, adding relief to global LNG markets
Qatar repositioning LNG tankers ahead of Hormuz reopening signals imminent resumption of Gulf LNG flows, weighing heavily on TTF
G7 escalation of sanctions on Russian gas exports represents a structural upside risk for European gas prices despite today's softness

power.summary: EU carbon EUAs held near flat on the day at $75.44/EUA (-0.17%) but remain the relative outperformer across the energy complex, up 3.05% on the week and 5.61% on the month. The divergence with TTF — down over 17% on both the week and month — is notable and may reflect regulatory and policy flows rather than pure fuel-switching economics. Key political developments include UK Prime Minister Starmer's pledge at the G7 of a £210 million nuclear energy support package for Ukraine alongside fresh Russia sanctions, signalling sustained Western commitment to low-carbon energy infrastructure. Poland has moved to tax windfall profits earned by fuel companies during the Iran war period. Supply-side headlines — the Hormuz reopening and Australian LNG resolution — are modestly bearish for gas-fired generation costs but have not yet pulled EUAs lower.
drivers: EU EUAs outperforming the broader energy selloff, up over 5% on the month, likely supported by policy demand and the EU's latest Russia sanctions package
UK's £210 million nuclear energy package for Ukraine signals continued G7 commitment to non-fossil power infrastructure
Poland's approval of a windfall tax on fuel companies that profited from the Iran war highlights regulatory risk now surfacing across European energy markets
